title: Best Alternatives to Scratch for iPad (2026 Guide)
summary: Compare Scratch, hyperPad, GDevelop, Hopscotch, and Swift Playgrounds by learning goal, iPad workflow, and the kind of project you want to build.
body_markdown:
Scratch is a free visual programming platform for creating interactive stories, games, and animations. It is a strong place to learn sequencing, events, variables, and conditions. If your main goal is to build and test a 2D game directly on iPad, you may want a tool with an iPad-focused game workflow.


This guide compares the intent of several options. It does not treat “more features” as automatically better. The right choice depends on whether you want to learn coding concepts, prototype a game on iPad, work across desktop and web, or learn a text-based language.


## Quick comparison


Tool Model Best fit


[Scratch](https://scratch.mit.edu/help/about/) Blocks Programming concepts


hyperPad Visual Behaviors 2D games on iPad


[GDevelop](https://gdevelop.io/) Events Cross-device projects


[Hopscotch](https://www.gethopscotch.com/) Blocks Introductory coding


[Swift Playgrounds](https://www.apple.com/swift/playgrounds/) Swift Typed programming


Product availability, export options, and prices can change. Check each product’s current page before choosing it for a class or long-term project.


## When Scratch is the right choice


Scratch is designed especially for young people, but people of all ages use it. Its official materials focus on creating interactive stories, games, and animations, then sharing them with the Scratch community.


Choose Scratch when your first goal is to understand how programming works. Its blocks make events, loops, variables, and conditions visible without requiring typed syntax.


A useful first Scratch project is a short game with one sprite, one input, one score variable, and one win condition. That is enough to practice logic without turning the lesson into a large production.


## When hyperPad is the better fit


Choose hyperPad when the project itself is the lesson: you want to arrange a Scene, add Objects, connect visual Behaviors, test the result on iPad, and keep expanding the game.


A similar first project in hyperPad might work like this:


1. Add a player Object and a coin Object to one Scene.
2. Add touch input that moves the player.
3. Detect a collision with the coin.
4. Increase a score Attribute.
5. Remove the coin and play a sound.
6. Show a message when the score reaches five.


That exercise covers input, events, actions, state, and debugging. The[Behavior Interface Overview](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/behavior-interface-overview) explains the visual editor. The[Interface Overview](https://www.hyperpad.com/documentation/interface-overview) covers the main game editor.


## Scratch and hyperPad are built for different outcomes


Question Scratch hyperPad


What do you build with? Programming blocks, sprites, and a stage Behaviors, Objects, Scenes, Graphics, and Attributes


What is the main starting point? Learn and practice programming concepts Build and test a 2D game on iPad


How is logic represented? Connected blocks Connected visual Behaviors


Where do you share first? Scratch online community hyperPad community and project workflow


Is typed code required for the core workflow? No No


Scratch is not a lesser tool because it has a different purpose. It remains useful for learning programming logic. hyperPad is the stronger match when the search intent is specifically “make a game on iPad” and you want an editor designed around that device.


## Other alternatives to consider


### GDevelop


GDevelop uses event-based logic and supports game creation across multiple environments. Review its current device support and export options if you expect to move between iPad, browser, and desktop.


### Hopscotch


Hopscotch focuses on learning to code through projects on iPad. It can suit younger learners who want a guided block-based experience before choosing a fuller game engine.


### Swift Playgrounds


Swift Playgrounds is for learning and using Swift. Choose it when typed programming is the goal. It is a different path from Scratch and hyperPad, not a direct replacement for either visual workflow.


## How to choose in 10 minutes


Use one small test instead of comparing long feature lists.


1. Pick one mechanic, such as moving to collect an item.
2. Try to build it in the tool.
3. Check whether you understand the logic after the first session.
4. Decide whether its sharing and publishing path matches your goal.
5. Keep the tool that helps you finish the next playable step.


For a classroom, also check account management, privacy requirements, device compatibility, and licensing before rollout.


## Common questions


### Is Scratch available for free?


Yes. Scratch says it is provided free of charge. Its official About page explains its learning and community purpose.


### Can I make a game on iPad without typing code?


Yes. Scratch, hyperPad, and other visual tools let you create logic without typing a traditional programming language. The workflows and publishing options differ.


### Is visual coding real programming?


Visual coding uses programming concepts such as events, actions, conditions, values, input, and state. It does not replace every text-based language, but it can teach the logic behind software and games.


### Which option should I start with?


Start with Scratch if your priority is learning programming concepts in a broad creative community. Start with hyperPad if your priority is building a playable 2D game directly on iPad.


Build one small mechanic in hyperPad Starter. If the Scene, Object, and Behavior workflow makes sense after that test, use it for your first complete game loop.
